cards.title: A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis

depth.text: a dermatologist found a specialist image model outdid two AI models at **spotting skin cancer**

On **200 biopsy-proven lesions**, the fine-tuned CNN got the right diagnosis for **125 (62%)**, compared with **84 and 85 (42%)** for the two LLMs. The author says every lesion had been biopsied, making the cases harder, and warns that 200 cases are too few to rank close results.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say narrow tasks are better handled by purpose-built classifiers; others say this test misses what LLMs could do with clinical notes, patient questions, or messier images.

comments.text: This is an example of why I'm a little stumped about why people are excited about Jev-style decision models. For any application at scale it'd be way more accurate to have a dedicated classifier using the right architecture (neural net, bayesian, etc.) LLMs drive the cost of making those models down to near zero. Just use the LLM to make a thing that's actually good at what you need it to do.

> I compared to a 10-year old CNN and to my surprise found that this was superior. I'm surprised he's surprised. > A small, old, specialised network using an outdated architecture recognises skin lesions far better than two frontier LLMs. Yes of course. A 30m params Katago network with one playout is superhuman in playing go, while frontier LLMs have over 10,000 times more parameters and aren't…

> I used Inception v3 pretrained on everyday photographs and then fine-tuned all layers on 68,011 dermoscopic and clinical images from the ISIC Archive on a single H100 GPU. >These 200 test lesions, and every other photograph of the same lesion or patient, were removed from its data (including the validation set) before training, so it had never seen them, and they were not used to choose the…

As people have mentioned, it isn't that surprising that a specially trained model beats a general purpose model. However, I think it kinda misses the potential of llms for diagnosis. What happens if we also include journal notes? What if we let the model generate questions to ask the patient and include those? What if the images aren't perfect examples and happen to contain out of distribution…
And a calculator outperforms LLMs at multiplication and division...

cards.title: The Goose Programming Language

depth.text: someone made **Goose**, a language where the compiler assigns **data stacks** for memory

One commenter says Goose suits programs with a **fixed number of growable memory regions**, but another asks how it handles arbitrary numbers of changing-size values without a heap. A commenter also warns that, with **no garbage collection**, stacks can keep growing even when old data is no longer used.

cards.camps: Two camps: skeptics say a fixed set of stacks may not handle arbitrary, changing-size values and argue a proper heap may be needed; supporters say Goose is fine for programs that can set the number of growable memory regions in advance.

cards.title: GPU-unlock: FP/BF16 instruction issue rate on Nvidia 3000's cards

depth.text: someone built a **Linux tool** that unlocks **faster math** on some Nvidia GeForce cards

The project says its module doubles **FP/BF16 FMA instruction issue speed** on GA102, GA103, GA104 and GA106 cards, loading before the unmodified NVIDIA driver. It reports faster **LLM prefill**, while decode and INT8 work stay about the same; commenters dispute what gets unlocked and how widely it has been tested.

cards.camps: Two camps: the project says it unlocks FP/BF16 instruction speed across four GPU families; one commenter says the claim is really about FP32 and says they have seen reports only for 3090/3090 Ti cards.

cards.title: Why is AI generated language so hard to understand?

depth.text: researchers found **AI writing** uses more **hard-to-process language**, perhaps because models optimize for tasks beyond communication

All **nine models** used more **inanimate subjects with animate verbs** and low-frequency n-grams than human writing; most also used longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation. The authors suggest that goals like math, code, and reasoning may favor **information density** over successful communication. They also found that fine-tuning a model with a length penalty led to language that diverged from human-like patterns.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say AI writing is hard to understand because it favors dense information; others say it’s just tedious, or that the bigger issue is whether it’s useful to its audience.
terms: inanimate subject with an animate verb

My guess is years of RLHF optimized for rater's first impressions of how well-written something was. It uses lists! It has headings! It uses fun phrases like 'smoking gun'! It's long and informative! At best it makes sentences weirdly ambiguous, at worst it makes them borderline incomprehensible, and it's…

LLMs are showing us that a lot of what we think of as cognition is actually part of the elaborate symbol system which is Language, as opposed to a property of "mind" (either biologically or artificially instantiated.) LLM-generated text is hard to understand because while it's perfectly good language that follows valid cognitive and informational patterns, it does not reflect the intent or mental…

Consider too that AI training corpuses include vast amounts of commercial speech which is designed to numb the critical faculties and produce action; likewise they include numerous opinion articles, which are designed to persuade and often leverage rhetorical fallacies, whether cynically or as a reflection of an author's imperfect thought process.

cards.title: The Goose Programming Language

depth.text: Goose is a **systems language** that stays **memory safe** without a heap or lifetime annotations

Goose stores dynamic values inline on **compiler-managed data stacks** and frees them when their scope ends; it also compiles to one C file. Its repository benchmarks report **3.3x the speed** of idiomatic C++, 1.16x hand-optimized C++, and 1.12x the best safe Rust, using **less memory**.

cards.title: Dream-1

depth.text: someone made a robot model that can control **new robots** doing **tasks it has never seen**

Dream Labs says **Dream-1** works through a public API with **bimanual robots** using parallel grippers, without robot-specific fine-tuning or demonstrations. It costs **$3 per hour** ($2 per hour for Dream-1-flash), but the post warns it isn't validated for safety-critical use.

cards.camps: Two camps: some are excited about robots taking on household chores; others say the demos don't show useful real-world automation yet.

comments.text: Tested one prompt in the playground ("Move the elephant next to the ball") and this is the generated recorded video link: https://dreamlabs.ai/playground/?play=a05f0e641559490e#sim

This is all very cool and something I would like to play with. However I also can’t mentally bridge this over to the actual automation, manufacturing, and warehouse work I’ve been involved with throughout my career. Everything about this looks optimized for getting-started tasks to play around with, but I’m left feeling that it’s not the right fit or even a good starting point for real automation…

Obviously AI written text. At least there is real content here, however I do find the order and the way in which it was written and portrayed to have a heavy AI smell. That is, it's hard to read and follow the clean narrative, it isn't written the way a human who was trying to convince another human would write, and is less effective because of it.

This post feels really weird, DreamLabs isn’t some well known project like Anthropic or OpenAI and Dream-1 wasn’t really an awaited release. But somehow this was pushed to the front page of HN before receiving a single comment with a title reminiscent of a major LLM release. Like I can only find 1 other reference historically to this lab and nobody noticed it or cared.

I don't like the direction this is going in - so a third party is going to be able to control a robot in my house? we shouldn't aim for economies of scale on this problem as there are massive negative externalities attached to it. Hopefully, a chinese lab will release an open source version soon.
